segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's design a distributed caching layer that sits between our services and the primary databases.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: First question, is this a cache aside design where the application manages it, or a read through cache that fronts the database?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Cache aside is the most common. The application checks the cache, and on a miss it reads the database and populates the cache.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: It is simple and the failure mode is benign. If the cache is unavailable, everything still works, just slower.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Read through hides the logic behind the cache client, which is cleaner, but it couples the cache to the data source.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For writes we have write through, write behind and simple invalidation. I would default to invalidation on write.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Agreed. Writing the new value into the cache on update creates a race where a concurrent stale read overwrites it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Deleting the entry instead means the next reader repopulates from the database, which is always correct if slightly slower.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: There is still a subtle race. A reader can load a value, then a writer updates and invalidates, then the reader writes its stale value.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That window is narrow but real. Techniques like delayed double deletion or versioned writes reduce it substantially.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Versioned values are cleaner. We store the row version with the cached value and refuse to overwrite a newer version.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's talk about distribution. How do we decide which node holds which key?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Naive modulo hashing on the node count remaps almost every key when the cluster size changes, which is catastrophic.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Consistent hashing fixes that. Keys and nodes map onto a ring, and adding a node only moves the keys in one arc.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: With virtual nodes, each physical node owns many points on the ring, which smooths out the distribution.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Without virtual nodes the load is quite uneven, because random placement of a few points leaves some arcs much larger than others.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A typical configuration uses a hundred or more virtual nodes per physical node to keep the variance acceptable.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Rendezvous hashing is an alternative that gives similar properties with simpler reasoning, though it is less common in practice.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Now eviction. When memory fills, which entries do we drop?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Least recently used is the default and works well for typical skewed access, but it is vulnerable to a large scan.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Right, one batch job reading a million cold keys can evict the entire hot working set, which we call cache pollution.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Least frequently used resists that, but it has the opposite problem. Old popular items linger after they stop being popular.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Segmented approaches solve both. A small probationary segment absorbs new entries, and only items accessed again get promoted.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That way a one time scan passes through the probationary area without disturbing the protected working set.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should also set a time to live on everything, even when we invalidate explicitly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Yes, the expiry is a safety net. If an invalidation is ever missed, the staleness is bounded rather than permanent.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's cover the three classic failure patterns. Cache penetration, cache breakdown and cache avalanche.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Penetration is when requests ask for keys that do not exist anywhere, so every request misses and hits the database.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The fix is to cache the negative result with a short expiry, or to use a bloom filter to reject impossible keys immediately.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Breakdown is when a single very hot key expires and thousands of concurrent requests all stampede to the database at once.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We solve that with a mutex, where only one request recomputes and the others wait briefly for the result.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Or with probabilistic early expiration, where requests randomly refresh the value shortly before it actually expires.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: I like that approach because it avoids the lock entirely and spreads the refresh load smoothly over time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Avalanche is when a large number of keys expire simultaneously, usually because they were all loaded together.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Adding random jitter to every expiry time prevents the synchronized wave, which is a one line fix with a large payoff.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Hot keys are the other operational headache. One key can exceed the throughput of the single node that owns it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Client side local caching of the hottest keys helps, with a very short lifetime to bound the staleness.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We can also replicate a hot key across several nodes with a suffix, and have clients pick one at random.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That multiplies read capacity for that key at the cost of more complex invalidation across all the replicas.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's discuss sizing. How do we decide how much memory the cache needs?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Start from the working set. Measure the distinct keys accessed in a representative window and multiply by the average entry size.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Then check the hit ratio curve. There is usually a knee where adding memory stops improving the hit rate meaningfully.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Serialization format matters too. A compact binary encoding can halve the memory compared to verbose text formats.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And compression for larger values, though we should measure, because the CPU cost can outweigh the memory savings for small entries.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: On availability, do we replicate the cache or treat node loss as acceptable?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: If the database can absorb the miss traffic from one lost node, replication is unnecessary complexity.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: But if the cache is load bearing, meaning the database cannot survive without it, we need replicas and a careful warm up procedure.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Cold start is genuinely dangerous there. Restarting an empty cache in front of a saturated database can take the whole system down.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Gradual warm up, admitting traffic slowly while the cache fills, is the safe procedure for that scenario.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: To summarize, cache aside with invalidation, consistent hashing with virtual nodes, segmented eviction and jittered expiry.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Plus negative caching, single flight refresh for hot keys, local client caches and a deliberate plan for cold start.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The general lesson is that a cache changes your failure modes as much as your performance, so both need design attention.
